title: Parameters
description: Hand values to a function so one function can do the job many ways.

content.value: Telling a Function What to Work With

items: A function with empty brackets always does exactly the same thing.
Put a variable declaration inside the brackets, like `int count`. That is a **parameter**: a variable that gets its value from the call.
The value the caller hands over, like the `3` in `printStars(3)`, is an **argument**.

content.real: A labelled envelope and the letter inside
content.text: The envelope's label, `name`, is the parameter: the slot. The letter you put in, `"Amara"`, is the argument: what goes in the slot.

steps.note: A call with the argument `"Amara"`. C++ jumps into `greet`.
The parameter `name` is created and filled with the argument.
Back in `main`. `name` is gone: it only lived inside the function. Now a second call.
The function ends and `name` disappears again.

content.title: Watch the argument travel in
content.outro: The parameter gets a new value on every call.

content.caption: One function, three different results. A function without parameters can only be reused. One with parameters can be adapted.

content.question: In `printStars(7)`, what is `7`?
content.explain: The value you hand over at the call is the argument. `int count` in the header is the parameter that receives it.

items: Each one needs its **own type**, even when two in a row share a type.
Arguments match parameters by **position**, not by name: first to first, second to second.

parts.label: 1st parameter
parts.note: Gets the first argument. Its type is `string`.

parts.label: 2nd parameter
parts.note: Gets the second argument. It needs its own type, `int`.

content.caption: Name parameters for what they mean inside the function, whatever the caller's variables are called.

items.title: Does not compile
items.text: Text cannot go into an `int` slot. C++'s type checking catches it.

content.title: Order matters
content.caption: Between number types C++ is more relaxed: `printStars(3.9)` compiles and the `double` is chopped to the int 3 on the way in. If decimals matter, make the parameter a `double`.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `10` goes into `a` and `3` goes into `b`, so the body works out `10 - 3`.

items: An argument does not have to be typed into your code.
Anything that gives a value of the right type works: a variable, a calculation, or something `cin` just read.
The function never knows where its values came from. That is what makes it reusable.

content.caption: Sample run: type `Mia` and `72`. It prints `Mia | #######` then `A pass.`

`cin` and `cout` work in every function, not just `main`. Both calls read from the same keyboard: whichever reads next carries on where the last read stopped. The `getline` trap still applies: after `cin >>`, call `cin.ignore()` before the next `getline`, in any function. Sample run: type `4` and `9`, it prints `First number doubled is 8` and `Second number doubled is 18`.

content.value: When you pass a variable, the function gets a **copy** of its value. Changing the copy does nothing to the original. This is called **pass by value**.

steps.note: Call `addTen`, handing over the value of `score`.
A new variable `number` starts as a copy: 50.
Inside the function it really is 60.
The function ended, so `number` vanished. `score` never moved.

content.title: Watch the copy change, not the original
content.outro: So `addTen(score);` on its own is almost always a bug. To get a value back, return it (next lesson). To really change the caller's variable, C++ has a way too, two lessons from now.

content.value: The copy rule makes functions safe. A function cannot reach out and quietly change your variables, so a bug in one function stays in that function.
content.title: Why this is good

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `n` is a copy of `x`. Setting the copy to `0` leaves `x` at 5.

content.value: C++ lets a parameter have a **default value**. If the caller leaves that argument out, the default fills the slot.

items.title: Does not compile
items.text: `length` comes after a default but has none.

items.title: Compiles
items.text: The parameter with a default is last.

content.title: Defaults go at the end
content.caption: Once one parameter has a default, every parameter after it needs one too.

items: With a prototype, write the default in the **prototype only**, not again in the definition.
Keep parameter lists short. One or two is comfortable, three is fine. Five is a function that wants splitting up.

content.question: Using the `printBar` above, what does `printBar(4);` print?
content.explain: `symbol` was left out, so it takes its default, `'*'`, and four of them are drawn.

practice.question: Write printRow(char symbol, int count) that prints that symbol that many times on one line, then call it three times with different symbols.
These three lines are the same code with different numbers. Replace them with one function plus three calls.
Write times(int a, int b) that prints a line like `3 x 4 = 12`, then use a loop in main to call it for the whole 6 times table.
This prints 50 both times. Add a comment explaining why the function cannot change main's variable.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
options: The parameter is the slot in the function, the argument is the value passed in
They are two words for the same thing
A parameter has a type, an argument does not
quiz.explain: `void printStars(int count)` declares the parameter. `printStars(7)` supplies the argument.

quiz.question: How does C++ decide which argument goes into which parameter?
options: By matching the types in any order
quiz.explain: The first argument fills the first parameter. Swap a number and a string and it will not compile, which is the good outcome.

quiz.question: A function changes the value of its plain `int` parameter. What happens to the caller's variable?
options: Nothing: the function was working on a copy
quiz.explain: That is pass by value. The parameter is a separate variable that started with the same value, and it disappears when the function ends.

quiz.question: Can a function other than main use `cin`?
options: Yes: every function can read, and the input carries on where the last read stopped
No, only main can read input
Yes, but each function gets its own fresh copy of the input
quiz.explain: There is one stream of input for the whole program. Whichever function reads next takes the next value.

quiz.question: Given `void printBar(int length, char symbol = '*')`, what does `printBar(4);` print?
options: Nothing, it does not compile without a second argument
quiz.explain: The missing argument is filled in by the default value, so symbol is '*' for this call.
